edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De resurrectione carnis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.locus: On the Resurrection of the Flesh I
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Fiducia Christianorum, resurrectio mortuorum. Illa credentes sumus; hoc credere veritas cogit. Veritatem Deus aperit; sed vulgus irridet, existimans nihil superesse post mortem; et tamen defunctis parentant, et quidem impensissimo officio, pro moribus eorum, pro temporibus esculentorum; ut quos negant sentire quicquam, escam desiderare praesumant. At ego magis ridebo vulgus, tunc quoque, cum ipsos defunctos atrocissime exurit, quos postmodum gulosissime nutrit, iisdem ignibus et promerens et offendens. O pietatem de crudelitate ludentem! sacrificat, an insultat, cum crematis cremat? Plane cum vulgo interdum et sapientes sententiam suam jungunt. Nihil esse post mortem Epicuri schola est. Ait et Seneca, omnia post mortem finiri, etiam ipsam. Satis est autem, si non minor philosophia Pythagorae et Empedocli. Sed et Platonici immortalem animam e contrario reclamant: imo adhuc proxime etiam in corpora remeabilem affirmant; etsi non in eadem, etsi non in humana tantummodo; ut Euphorbus in Pythagoram, Homerus in pavum recenseantur. Certe recidivatum animae corporalem pronuntiaverunt; tolerabilius mutata, quam negata qualitate: pulsata saltem, licet non adita veritate. Ita saeculum resurrectionem mortuorum, nec cum errat, ignorat.
pass_a_gloss: The confidence of Christians is the resurrection of the dead; we are believers in that; this truth compels us to believe; God reveals the truth; but the crowd mocks, thinking nothing remains after death; and yet they pay respects to the dead, and indeed with very expensive duty, according to their customs, at the times of feasts; so that they presume to desire food on the basis that they desire food, whom they deny feel anything; but I will laugh at the crowd even then, when it also most atrociously burns the dead, whom afterwards it most greedily nourishes, both earning and offending with the same fires; O piety playing with cruelty; does it sacrifice or insult, when it burns the cremated; plainly even the wise sometimes join their opinion with the crowd; the school of Epicurus is that nothing exists after death; and Seneca says that all things, even the soul, end after death; but it is enough if not lesser philosophy is that of Pythagoras and Empedocles; and the Platonists on the other hand claim that the soul is immortal; indeed they even affirm that it is still capable of returning into bodies; although not into the same, although not only into human ones; so that Euphorbus is reckoned into Pythagoras, and Homer into a peacock; certainly they have proclaimed the recurrence of the soul into a body; more tolerable with a changed quality, than with a denied one; at least struck by, even if not reached by the truth; thus the age does not ignore the resurrection of the dead, even when it errs
pass_b_english: The confidence of Christians rests on the resurrection of the dead. We believe it; truth itself compels us to. God reveals the truth, but the crowd mocks it, convinced that nothing survives death. Yet they still pay their respects to the dead, and at ruinous expense, following their customs and the calendar of feasts. They presume that those they insist feel nothing somehow desire food — as if appetite could exist without a subject to feel it. I will laugh at the crowd even then, when it incinerates the dead with savage brutality, only to gorge itself on them afterward, using the same fires to both cremate and cook. O piety sporting with cruelty! Is it sacrifice or insult, when it burns what has already been burned? Even the wise sometimes throw in their lot with the mob. The Epicurean school teaches that nothing exists after death. Seneca agrees: everything ends at death, the soul included. But Pythagorean and Empedoclean philosophy is no lightweight either. The Platonists, conversely, insist the soul is immortal; indeed, they claim it can still migrate into other bodies — though not the same ones, and not only human ones — so that Euphorbus passes into Pythagoras, Homer into a peacock. They have proclaimed the soul's return to a body; a changed condition is more tolerable than a denied one: at least they have been struck by the truth, even if they have not reached it. Thus the age does not ignore the resurrection of the dead, even when it goes astray.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant interpretive additions and shifts in meaning that are not present in the Latin source or the Pass A gloss. Specifically, 'using the same fires to both cremate and cook' (Latin: 'iisdem ignibus et promerens et offendens') adds 'cook' which is not in the text; 'offendens' is more likely 'offering' (as in an offering/sacrifice) or 'offending' in a moral sense, but 'cook' is an interpretive leap. Furthermore, 'as if appetite could exist without a subject to feel it' is a massive expansion of 'ut quos negant sentire quicquam, escam desiderare praesumant'. Most critically, 'at least they have been struck by the truth' (Pass B) contradicts the Latin 'licet non adita veritate' and Pass A 'even if not reached by the truth', which implies they have *not* yet been reached/attained by the truth, whereas Pass B suggests they have been 'struck' by it.
reasons: Pass B adds 'as if appetite could exist without a subject to feel it' which is not in the Latin 'ut quos negant sentire quicquam, escam desiderare praesumant'.
Pass B adds 'cook' to 'iisdem ignibus et promerens et offendens', which is not in the source.

Pass B translates 'licet non adita veritate' as 'at least they have been struck by the truth', which reverses the meaning of the negation in the Latin (they have *not* been reached/attained by the truth).

review.notes: source: 'escam desiderare praesumant'; English: 'presume to desire food'
